parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
The first law of thermodynamics may be expressed as $$\Delta U = (+q) + (+w)$$ where $\Delta U$ is the increase in internal energy of the system.

State the meaning of:
hints: Hint 1: Think about what can change the stored energy of a gas - heating it and squeezing or letting it expand are two different routes.
Hint 2: The + sign means energy is going into the system, so link +q to heating the system and +w to compressing the system by an outside force.
parts.proper_answer: +q is the thermal energy transferred to the system. +w is the work done on the system.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Delta U Means**
Internal energy $U$ of an ideal gas is the total kinetic energy of its molecules. It only goes up if extra energy is put into the system from outside.

Step 2: **Two Ways To Add Energy**
You can add energy by heating, so $+q$ is energy in by thermal transfer to the system. You can also add energy by pushing a piston in, so $+w$ is energy in by work done on the system. Both make $\Delta U$ positive: $$\Delta U = (+q) + (+w)$$

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
The variation with pressure $p$ of the volume $V$ of a fixed mass of an ideal gas is shown in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

Fig. 2.1

The gas undergoes a cycle of changes A to B to C to A.

During the change A to B, the volume of the gas increases from $2.3 \times 10^{-3} \text{m}^3$ to $3.8 \times 10^{-3} \text{m}^3$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Show that the magnitude of the work done during the change A to B is $390 \text{J}$.
hints: Hint 1: Look closely at the line A to B in Fig. 2.1 - check what happens to $p$ while $V$ increases, and note the start and finish values of $V$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot Constant Pressure Expansion**
From A to B the pressure stays at $p = 2.6 \times 10^5\text{ Pa}$ while volume grows. For constant pressure, the magnitude of work is pressure times volume change.

Step 2: **Put In The Numbers**
$$W = p\Delta V$$ $$W = 2.6 \times 10^5 \times (3.8 \times 10^{-3} - 2.3 \times 10^{-3})$$ $$W = 2.6 \times 10^5 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3} = 390\text{ J}$$ This is work done by the gas as it expands, so work done on the gas would be $-390\text{ J}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State and explain the total change, if any, in the internal energy of the gas during one complete cycle.

markscheme_points.text: gas returns to its original temperature

hints: Hint 1: After one full cycle A to B to C to A, compare the final pressure and volume with the starting pressure and volume.
Hint 2: Recall what controls the internal energy of a fixed mass of ideal gas, and what that implies if the start and end states are identical.
parts.proper_answer: No total change in internal energy. The gas returns to its original state so returns to its original temperature, and $U$ depends only on temperature.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **A Cycle Returns To Start**
A to B to C to A ends exactly where it began at A, so $p$ and $V$ are the same as at the start. From $pV = nRT$, the temperature $T$ must also be the same.

Step 2: **Internal Energy Follows Temperature**
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature. Same temperature means same internal energy, so over one complete cycle: $$\Delta U_{total} = 0$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
During the change A to B, $1370 \text{J}$ of thermal energy is transferred to the gas.

During the change B to C, no thermal energy enters or leaves the gas. The work done on the gas during this change is $550 \text{J}$.

Use these data and the information in (b) to complete Table 2.1.

Table 2.1

markscheme_points.text: A to B row all correct (1370, -390, 980)
B to C row all correct (0, 550, 550)
C to A row: ΔU adds to the other two ΔU values to give zero
C to A row: w = 0 and q adds to w to give ΔU value
markscheme_points.guidance: complete correct answer: change | q / J | w / J | ΔU / J; A to B | (+)1370 | -390 | (+)980; B to C | 0 | (+)550 | (+)550; C to A | -1530 | 0 | -1530

hints: Hint 1: Start with A to B - you know heat in is 1370 J and the gas expands, so decide the sign of $w$ for work done on the gas.
Hint 2: For B to C no heat flows, so think about how $q$, $w$ and $\Delta U$ must be related when $q = 0$.
Hint 3: For C to A the volume does not change, so consider what that tells you about work done.
Hint 4: Use the fact that the three $\Delta U$ values must add to zero for the whole cycle to find the missing C to A change.
parts.proper_answer: A to B: $q = +1370\text{ J}$, $w = -390\text{ J}$, $\Delta U = +980\text{ J}$. B to C: $q = 0$, $w = +550\text{ J}$, $\Delta U = +550\text{ J}$. C to A: $q = -1530\text{ J}$, $w = 0$, $\Delta U = -1530\text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **A to B - Heated Expansion**
Heat to gas $q = +1370\text{ J}$. Gas expands and does $390\text{ J}$ of work, so work done on gas is negative: $w = -390\text{ J}$. First law gives: $$\Delta U = q + w = 1370 - 390 = +980\text{ J}$$

Step 2: **B to C - Adiabatic Compression**
No thermal transfer so $q = 0$. Work done on gas $w = +550\text{ J}$. Then: $$\Delta U = 0 + 550 = +550\text{ J}$$ Internal energy rises because work is done on the gas.

Step 3: **C to A - Constant Volume Cooling**
Volume stays at $2.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$, so no work is done: $w = 0$. Let the unknown be $\Delta U_{CA}$. For a cycle total $\Delta U = 0$: $$980 + 550 + \Delta U_{CA} = 0$$ $$\Delta U_{CA} = -1530\text{ J}$$

Step 4: **Find Heat For C to A**
Apply $\Delta U = q + w$ with $w = 0$: $$-1530 = q + 0$$ $$q = -1530\text{ J}$$ Negative means thermal energy leaves the gas as it is cooled at constant volume back to A.
